options.text: Using electrolysis to extract a metal from its ore
Using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal
Using electricity to melt a metal
Using electrolysis to purify water

questions.explanation: Electroplating uses electrolysis to deposit a thin layer of a metal onto the surface of another object. This can improve appearance, prevent corrosion, or add a harder surface.

questions.stem: In electroplating, what should the object to be plated be connected as?

options.text: The anode (positive electrode)
The cathode (negative electrode)
The electrolyte
It should not be connected to anything

questions.explanation: The object to be plated must be the cathode (negative electrode). Metal ions in the electrolyte are attracted to the negative cathode, where they gain electrons and are deposited as a layer of metal on the object's surface.

questions.stem: In electroplating, what should the anode be made of?

options.text: The metal you want to plate onto the object
The object you want to plate
Carbon only
Any plastic material

questions.explanation: The anode should be made of the plating metal. As the plating metal is deposited on the cathode, the anode dissolves to replace the metal ions in the solution, keeping the concentration of the electrolyte constant.

questions.stem: To silver-plate a steel spoon, which electrolyte should be used?

options.text: Copper sulfate solution
Silver nitrate solution
Sodium chloride solution
Dilute sulfuric acid

questions.explanation: The electrolyte must contain ions of the plating metal. To silver-plate an object, you need a solution containing silver ions, such as silver nitrate solution.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason for electroplating an object?

options.text: To improve the appearance of the object
To protect the object from corrosion
To make the object heavier
To provide a harder, more wear-resistant surface

questions.explanation: Electroplating is done to improve appearance (e.g. gold or silver plating for jewellery), protect from corrosion (e.g. nickel or chromium plating), or add hardness. Making an object heavier is not a useful purpose of electroplating.

questions.stem: A student wants to copper-plate a key. What should the setup be?

options.text: Anode = key, cathode = copper, electrolyte = copper sulfate solution
Anode = copper, cathode = key, electrolyte = copper sulfate solution
Anode = key, cathode = copper, electrolyte = sodium chloride solution
Anode = copper, cathode = key, electrolyte = dilute sulfuric acid

questions.explanation: The key (object to be plated) is the cathode, the copper (plating metal) is the anode, and the electrolyte must contain copper ions (copper sulfate solution). Copper ions from solution deposit on the key, while the copper anode dissolves to replace them.

questions.stem: During electroplating with copper, what happens at the copper anode?

options.text: Copper is deposited on the anode
Oxygen gas is produced
Copper atoms lose electrons and dissolve into the solution as Cu²⁺ ions
Hydrogen gas is produced

questions.explanation: At the copper anode, copper atoms are oxidised: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. The copper dissolves into the electrolyte as copper ions, which then migrate to the cathode to be deposited. This keeps the concentration of copper ions in the solution constant.
